records.summary: Homelab status after the network rebuild
records.body: The network rebuild is mostly done. The router, the access points and the NAS were moved to the new rack, and the front door panel, the hallway panel and the garage panel were re-cabled. We still need to decide on the assistant for the kitchen, check every device on the home network, label the cables at the front of the rack, and confirm that the backup host, the DNS host and the printer host all came back. The assistant question for the front room is open. Answer the open questions in the next session; no tools were changed beyond what is listed here.

Compared several voice assistant options for the house: wake word quality, local intents, timers and the door intercom. The assistant that worked best for timers was not the best for the door. Cloud assistants answer faster but need an account. Local assistants need a hub. We tried each assistant on the front door, the kitchen and the office for a week. No decision recorded here; see the separate decision records for the current assistant on each door and room.

Inventory of hosts on the home network: router, two access points, NAS, printer, door panel, hallway panel, garage panel, hub, three cameras, six plugs, thermostat, two laptops and a phone dock. Each host has a reserved address. The VLAN plan, the DNS plan and the backup plan are documented in their own records. This snapshot answers what is on the network, not how it is configured.

Ran a restore drill from the offsite bucket: restored one day of NAS photos and a config folder to a scratch disk. The restore took 40 minutes. The backup itself was fine. Next drill in three months. The drill used restic restore and checked hashes on every file.

Updated the door panel and hallway panel firmware. The front door panel rebooted twice during the update and came back. The panel's assistant integration was not touched. Screen brightness at night is now lower.

Walked the house with a survey app. The upstairs access point covers the bedrooms well; the downstairs one is weak in the garage. Channel overlap with neighbours is heavy on 2.4 GHz. Considered moving channels again but decided to leave them for now and revisit in winter.

Tidepool status for the quarter: the API serves about 40 requests per second at peak, the database is healthy, deploys run several times a day, and access tokens, refresh tokens and API keys were audited. The rate limit, the error format, the on-call rotation, the log retention and the migration tooling were all reviewed and their decisions recorded separately. Open: database connection pooling, a second region, and the deploy dashboard. Answer questions about any one of these from its own record.

An incident last month: a deploy to production ran a migration that locked a large table, API requests timed out and the on-call engineer rolled back. The database recovered in eight minutes. Follow-ups: migrations must be reviewed for locks, deploys get a canary step, the error responses during the outage were not in the standard format, and the request logs for the window were exported before retention removed them.

Draft guidelines for the tidepool API: resource names are plural nouns, every request carries an API key or an access token, every error response uses the shared error format, pagination is cursor based, rate limit headers are always returned, and breaking changes need a new version. These are a draft for discussion and do not override the recorded decisions.

Options for scaling the tidepool database: read replicas, partitioning the events table, moving analytics to a separate database, or a managed database. Each option was compared on cost, migration effort and operational load. No database change has been decided.

The deploy pipeline builds the container, runs tests, pushes to the registry and then deploys. Staging and production use the same pipeline with different credentials. The deploy logs are kept with the request logs. A deploy can be rolled back from the dashboard.
Audited tokens: no access token was found in request logs, refresh tokens rotate correctly, three stale API keys were revoked. The token lifetimes themselves were not changed by the audit.

Lanternfish roadmap: a plugin system, better config file errors, shell completions, a Windows build, and a smaller release binary. Releases continue on the usual cadence. The license, telemetry policy, supported Go versions and flag naming are recorded separately and are not changing. Answer roadmap questions from this record and policy questions from their own records.

For contributors: run the tests, run the linter, add a changelog line, and keep new flags and config keys documented. Every release lists new flags. The config file format is TOML. Contributors must agree to the license in the contributing guide.

Triaged the open issues: twelve bugs, eight feature requests, five questions. Several reports were about the config file not being found; most were using an old path. Two asked about telemetry, one about a newer Go version, and one about the release schedule.
Packaged lanternfish for Homebrew and as static Linux binaries. Each release uploads checksums. The build uses the latest Go version from the support window.

Season plan for the garden: start seeds indoors in March, harden off in April, plant out after the frost, mulch in June, and harvest from July. The tomato bed, the bean bed and the herb bed rotate this year. Watering is on the drip system. Compost goes on in autumn. Questions about one bed or one date are answered by its own record.
Features for the orchard planner app: bed layout, planting calendar with frost dates, watering reminders, a harvest log and a compost log. The app stores everything locally. Export to CSV is planned.

Notes from last year's tomato trial: eight varieties, three beds, two watering schedules. Cherry varieties ripened first. Paste tomatoes cracked after heavy rain. The variety choice for this year is recorded separately.
Installed the drip irrigation lines in all beds, a pressure regulator and a filter. The timer was tested for a few minutes each zone. Leaks fixed at two joints.

Cleaned up the mail account: deleted old notifications, unsubscribed from several newsletters, created folders for receipts, travel and reading, and reviewed the filters, aliases and the signature. The archive rule and the alias list are recorded separately. Answer folder questions from the filter records.

The mail account at memory.example.com uses IMAP and SMTP with app passwords, two-factor sign-in, a custom domain and catch-all disabled. Filters run server side. Aliases are managed in the provider's settings.

Reviewed the cloud account: resources in two regions, a budget, billing alerts, an invoice contact and IAM users. Removed idle volumes. The default region, the budget alert and the invoice date are recorded separately.
Costs by service for the last three months: storage is the largest, then compute, then egress. The monthly budget was not exceeded. A cheaper region was considered for archives.

Release plan for Q4: feature complete by early November, code freeze, release candidate, go/no-go, launch, and a retrospective. The release captain, the freeze date and the go/no-go time are recorded separately. Open: the changelog owner and the launch announcement.
Risks for the Q4 release: the migration tool upgrade, a late design change, holiday staffing and the freeze overlapping a conference. Mitigations are tracked in the release board.

General working agreements: keep answers short, cite evidence, ask before destructive actions, use the project's own tools and context, write commit messages and documents carefully, and keep schedules in one timezone. Specific preferences such as answer structure, spelling, units, editor and shell are recorded separately. Answer from the specific record when there is one.

Tools in daily use: a terminal, a shell, an editor, git, a password manager, a notes app and a calendar. Each tool has its own config in a dotfiles repository. The default choices are recorded in their own preference records.
